extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, postdocs, and aspiring/early-career mathematicians
extracted.subtask_description: Practical career- and study-oriented advice for mathematics students and early-career researchers, including methods for learning proofs, study/note-taking strategies, research-productivity tips, and career-planning guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruct proofs yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to reconstruct the proof yourself. Usually you’ll be able to get halfway through the proof but get stuck on a key point. After you get frustrated, this is the time to uncover the proof, at which point you should quickly see the trick or observation that eluded you before, and then the rest of the proof often becomes quite obvious to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When done this way, the only thing you need to remember to reconstruct the proof is that key insight, which tends to stay in one’s memory precisely because you didn’t have it before.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach or adapt proofs to learn them deeply
rubrics_metrics.description: The very best ways to learn the proof of X are to teach about it in a class, or to adapt that proof for one’s own research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These options produce the deepest learning, though they are rarely available at the undergraduate level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check statements on a dense class of test objects then take limits
rubrics_metrics.description: "Check the statement for a dense class of test objects first, and then take limits" (suggested as a problem-solving strategy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strategy is useful in analysis and is connected to heuristics like L'Hôpital's rule and the Stolz–Cesàro theorem; use dense/test objects to get intuition and then pass to limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active study / note-taking strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Different methods of studying lecture notes: (1) re-read notes passively; (2) use scratch paper and take extra notes that may include 2a. typing up definitions, 2b. trying to solve theorems/propositions before reading solutions, 2c. working out your own examples, 2d. retyping notes to make them tidy/readable, 2e. something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retyping (2d) takes you through notes slowly and you learn a lot but it is time-consuming; passive re-reading (1) is fast but likely yields lower retention. The 'best' method depends on the individual and time constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a network of colleagues and collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively build your own network of colleagues and collaborators as part of career development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Networking is presented as a key, practical piece of career advice alongside other activities that promote success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a flexible career plan
rubrics_metrics.description: When it comes to graduate careers, don’t jump in blind. Have a plan so that you have some kind of structure but at the same time, don’t worry if you have to stray from that plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The only thing worse than jumping in without a plan is ploughing on with a plan that’s going to make you unhappy; be prepared to change course as circumstances dictate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend talks, write papers, and take initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend seminars/talks, write papers, and take initiative as actions that promote future success in research careers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities are singled out as particularly important for graduate-level students to promote visibility, productivity, and career progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and relearn your field continuously
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously learn and relearn the material in your field; keep revisiting foundational concepts as you progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This habit is useful across career stages and particularly valuable at postdoctoral level; advice may be tiered by career stage but the principle persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematics opportunistically; master core tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mathematics on an 'opportunistic' and 'need to know' basis: master a set of core tools so you can learn other techniques as required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For researchers who cannot spend all their time studying math, focus on core tools that allow you to approach other fields as needed; develop the ability to pick up additional methods when they become necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expository writing aids learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Expository writing is important for learning and understanding mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing to explain ideas (exposition) both clarifies your own thinking and aids retention; the blog references expository writing as a tool for learning.
